definition: In machine learning and data mining, a string kernel is a kernel function that operates on strings, i.e.
details: finite sequences of symbols that need not be of the same length. String kernels can be intuitively understood as functions measuring the similarity of pairs of strings: the more similar two strings a and b are, the higher the value of a string kernel K(a, b) will be. Using string kernels with kernelized learning algorithms such as support vector machines allow such algorithms to work with strings, without having to translate these to fixed-length, real-valued feature vectors. String kernels are used in domains where sequence data are to be clustered or classified, e.g. in text mining and gene analysis.

explainer.lead: A string kernel is a kernel function that operates on strings, finite symbol sequences that need not share a length. It matters because kernelized learners such as SVMs can then work directly on strings without fixed-length feature vectors.

tiers.eli5: Like a scoring rule that says how alike two words or sentences are, so you can compare them without first converting each into a list of numbers.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers pair string kernels with kernelized algorithms like SVMs to classify text or sequences directly. Pitfall: the similarity computation can be expensive on long strings, and results hinge on the chosen kernel.
tiers.paperLevel: A kernel function operating on strings that measures similarity of pairs, so that K(a, b) is higher for more similar strings a and b. It lets kernelized algorithms such as support vector machines handle strings without translation to fixed-length real-valued feature vectors.

explainer.example: An SVM with a string kernel classifies protein sequences by comparing pairs of symbol strings directly, without building fixed-length numeric features.
